# Lab 1 Report: Agent Pipeline (Exploring 4 Categories of Built-in Newsgroup)

**Data loading and cleaning checks.**\
I loaded document from four categories in the built-in 20-newsgroups data (`alt.atheism`, `comp.graphics`, `sci.med`, `soc.religion.christian`) with `load_dataset_tool` (`load_dataset_1`), giving 2,257 documents: 599 `soc.religion.christian`, 594 `sci.med`, 584 `comp.graphics` and 480 `alt.atheism`. `check_missing_tool` (`check_missing_4`) and `check_duplicates_tool` (`check_duplicates_5`) both returned 0, so no rows needed cleaning. `describe_data_tool` (`describe_data_6`) showed that documents are long-tailed: the overall mean length is about 1,993 characters but the median is 1,235, with a maximum of 60,713. `comp.graphics` has the shortest posts (mean 1,557, median 883) while `soc.religion.christian` has the longest (mean 2,263, median 1,649). This fits the domain: graphics posts are mostly short technical questions, while religious posts are long debates. Every category has large outliers (see the box-plot below).

![Document length by category](../plots/高俐雅_agentic-pipeline_plot_describe_data_6.png)

**Tokenization, document-term matrix and variance filtering.**\
I tokenized all documents into unigrams (`tokenize_8`) and built a count-based document-term matrix (`build_dtm_10`) with 35,788 terms, 365,886 non-zero entries and 99.55% sparsity. Stop words were not removed, so `term_frequency_tool` (`term_frequency_11`) is topped by "the" (29,825), "of" (17,660) and "to" (17,222), with "edu" (4,675) also in the top 20. The heatmap slices (`dtm_heatmap_12`, `dtm_heatmap_13`) show a nearly all-zero 20x20 corner. The sparsity comes mainly from rare terms (numbers, typos, header tokens), not from stop words, which are dense.

![DTM heatmap, first 20 documents x first 20 terms](../plots/高俐雅_agentic-pipeline_plot_dtm_heatmap_13.png)

`variance_filter_tool` with threshold 0.0 (`variance_filter_14`) removed nothing (35,788 kept), and threshold 0.01 (`variance_filter_15`) kept 5,354 terms and removed 30,434. The top kept terms were still stop words ("the", "of", "to", "and"...). The feature correlation matrix (`feature_correlation_20`) confirms why: the top-variance terms are almost all stop words that correlate strongly with each other (e.g. "the" and "of" at 0.9442), because their counts scale with document length. A domain term like "jpeg" correlates much less with them (0.2836 with "the"). These results really emphasize the need of removing stop words during tokenization process. In this particular session, DTM tool was made following the tool's contract that intentionally keep the English stop words inside the dataframes. 

![Correlation of top-variance terms](../plots/高俐雅_agentic-pipeline_plot_feature_correlation_20.png)

**Correlation-based term selection.**\
To find class-specific vocabulary I ran one-vs-rest Pearson and Spearman filters. I tried to analyze 2 categories: `comp.graphics` and `alt.atheism`. For `comp.graphics`, the results from 2 methods are noticeably different, probably due to sensitivity of outliers. Pearson (`pearson_filter_16`) resulted in conversational and header-like terms ("thanks" 0.2778, "keywords", "looking", "vga", "video"), while Spearman (`spearman_filter_17`) surfaced topical words led by "graphics" (0.5211), then "files", "image", "3d" and "program". For `alt.atheism`, both methods ranked "keith", "cco", "schneider", "allan" and "caltech" near the top (`pearson_filter_18`, `spearman_filter_19`), which indicates one prolific poster dominates that category. Spearman additionally brought in "atheists" (0.4276), "atheism", "islamic" and "morality", whereas Pearson included "livesey", "writes", "solntze" and "wpd". Spearman correlation method therefore gave the more meaningful terms on this dataset.

![Spearman, comp.graphics](../plots/高俐雅_agentic-pipeline_plot_turn130.png)
![Spearman, alt.atheism](../plots/高俐雅_agentic-pipeline_plot_turn134.png)

**Pattern mining.**\
Since Term-Frequency or Variance filtering methods might not work well in this dataset because of the high amount of stop words, I tried mining text pattern with `mine_patterns_tool` using TF-IDF filtering. Top-k (k=10) on `sci.med` (`mine_patterns_21`) and `soc.religion.christian` (`mine_patterns_22`) returned only header words and their combinations, e.g. "subject" (support 594), "lines" (585) and "organization" (582) in `sci.med`, and "lines", "subject" (both 599) in `soc.religion.christian`. FP-Growth on `alt.atheism` with min support 48 (`mine_patterns_23`) produced 181,199 patterns, and on `comp.graphics` with min support 100 (`mine_patterns_24`) produced 451. The sampled patterns were again mostly header tokens (plus words like "mail" and "image"). The patterns mostly capture the shared Usenet header format rather than discussion content. This implies another need for data cleaning, where headers should be stripped before mining or modelling.

**Dimensionality reduction, binarization and similarity.**\
`reduce_dimensions_tool` with UMAP (`reduce_dimensions_25`, 2,257 documents reduced to 2 dimensions, random_state=42) shows `comp.graphics` concentrated in the lower right and a small `sci.med` group at the far left. The two religion categories overlap heavily in the upper-left and middle of the plot, with `alt.atheism` points spread toward the right. Overall, the four categories are only partly separable, and the religious pair is the hardest to tell apart due to their similar domains. `binarize_labels_tool` (`binarize_labels_26`) produced a 2,257x4 one-hot label matrix. `cosine_similarity_tool` gave 0.5848 between documents 2 (`soc.religion.christian`) and 7 (`sci.med`) (`cosine_similarity_28`), and 0.2285 between the first and last documents (`cosine_similarity_29`). The first score is high for two unrelated topics, consistent with similarity being inflated by shared stop words in an unfiltered count matrix. Together these results point to the same preprocessing needs: remove stop words and headers, and use TF-IDF or rank-based measures before similarity, mining or classification.

![UMAP of documents by category](../plots/高俐雅_agentic-pipeline_plot_reduce_dimensions_25.png)
